questions.q: How is an IAM role fundamentally different from an IAM user?
options: A role has no password or permanent access keys — it's assumed temporarily rather than owned permanently
A role can only be used by the root user
A role has unlimited permissions by default
A role is identical to a user except for its name
questions.explain: Roles are assumed by a trusted entity for a limited time; they don't carry permanent credentials the way an IAM user does.

questions.q: What does a role's trust policy define?
options: Exactly who or what (a user, application, or AWS service) is allowed to assume the role
The maximum dollar amount the role can spend
Which AWS region the role operates in
The password required to use the role
questions.explain: The trust policy is separate from the role's permission policy and controls who can assume it in the first place.

questions.q: What does AWS STS (Security Token Service) do when a role is assumed?
options: Issues temporary credentials — an access key, secret key, and session token — valid for a limited time window
Permanently deletes the role after one use
Creates a brand-new IAM user automatically
Emails the account's root user for approval
questions.explain: STS issues short-lived credentials that expire automatically, removing the need for manual key rotation or cleanup.

questions.q: In the EC2-to-S3 example, how does the application reach S3 without an embedded access key?
options: A role with S3 permissions is attached to the EC2 instance as an instance profile, and AWS manages temporary credentials automatically
The access key is hardcoded into the application but encrypted
The application logs in as the root user each time
S3 allows anonymous access by default
questions.explain: Attaching a role via an instance profile means no long-lived key is ever generated or stored on the instance.

questions.q: Why do long-lived IAM user access keys carry more risk than role-based temporary credentials?
options: Long-lived keys keep working until manually deactivated, so if leaked (e.g., in a public repo), they remain usable indefinitely
Long-lived keys automatically expire every 15 minutes, same as role credentials
Long-lived keys cannot be used for any AWS API calls
There is no actual difference in risk between the two
questions.explain: A leaked long-lived key keeps working for whoever has it until someone notices and deactivates it; temporary role credentials expire on their own.
